lesson.title: Sort First, Ask Nothing Later: How DiffServ Scales Priority to the Whole Internet
lesson.summary: Differentiated Services (DiffServ) marks each packet with a coarse priority class using a small field in the IP header, letting every router along the path give it consistent treatment without ever tracking individual flows.
lesson.body:
QoS's goal, established earlier, is to prioritize traffic, but doing that at the scale of the actual internet rules out anything that requires bookkeeping per individual flow. A single core router can carry millions of concurrent flows passing through it at once, and that specific scaling wall is exactly what the next chapter's architecture, Integrated Services, runs into. DiffServ's answer to the same underlying goal is almost the opposite approach: don't track flows at all, just mark packets and read the marks.

The mechanism is deliberately simple. DiffServ repurposes six bits of what used to be IPv4's Type of Service byte, and the equivalent Traffic Class field in IPv6, into what is called a Differentiated Services Code Point, or DSCP. Devices at the edge of the network classify traffic, for example by application, by source, or by a customer's contracted service tier, and stamp a DSCP value onto each packet once, as it enters the network. Every router downstream from that point simply reads the DSCP value already present in the header and applies whatever Per Hop Behavior, or PHB, is locally configured for that value. There is no lookup of which specific flow a packet belongs to, no per-flow state retained anywhere, and no admission control check performed, just a small, fixed table along the lines of DSCP value X means apply PHB Y here. A handful of standard PHBs are actually defined and used in practice: Expedited Forwarding, aimed at low latency and low jitter traffic such as voice, several Assured Forwarding classes offering different relative levels of protection from being dropped under congestion, and an ordinary default PHB for everything else, which is just best-effort forwarding.

It is worth being explicit that DiffServ does not invent new scheduling mechanisms of its own. A Per Hop Behavior is implemented locally using exactly the scheduling disciplines covered earlier, for instance Expedited Forwarding traffic might be served through a strict priority queue while several Assured Forwarding classes share a weighted fair queue beneath it. DiffServ's actual contribution is standardizing what the markings mean across administrative boundaries, not the mechanics of moving packets off a queue.

The honest trade-off is that, because there is no admission control and no hard per-flow reservation, DiffServ can only offer relative, statistical guarantees, this class generally receives better treatment than that one, rather than IntServ's precise numeric guarantees, this exact flow is assured at least this much bandwidth and at most this much delay. An operator has to provision capacity for each class based on expected or measured demand, and service can still degrade under a badly underestimated overload. But no router anywhere in the path needs to remember any individual flow to get this benefit, and that single property is precisely why DiffServ, unlike IntServ, has actually been deployable across the real internet's core rather than staying confined to smaller networks.
